data.cultural_impact: The name Bhagram holds significant cultural importance in Hindu tradition. It is believed that this name was derived from the Sanskrit word 'Bhag', which means 'to share' or 'to possess'. In Hindu mythology, the deity Bhagavan represents the supreme being who distributes liberally, showering all his blessings on his devotees. The name Bhagram may be seen as an embodiment of this deity, symbolizing the distribution of strength, power, and wisdom to those around them.

historical_references.reference: Bhagavan Bhagram was a Jain Tirthankara. He is known as the sixth of twenty-four Tirthankaras in the current cycle of time (Avasarpini) in Jainism. Bhagavan Bhagram was born in the Ikshvaku dynasty in the city of Bhagapur in Magadh Desh, present day Bihar, India. His father was a sage named Ajat Shatru and his mother was a laywoman named Sati Kaur. Bhagavan Bhagram became a monk at the age of thirty and renounced the world under the Jain teacher, Bhagavan Rishabhanatha. He achieved Kevala Jnana at the age of forty-two and attained Nirvana at the age of forty-eight.

Bhagaram was a Hindu king who ruled over the region of Avantika in Malwa, present day Madhya Pradesh, India around 300 BCE. He was a contemporary of Alexander the Great. Bhagaram's military strength and strategic position allowed him to resist the Macedonian invasion. He is described as a just and generous king who ruled with the consent of his people.
